st.headline: Nvidia’s next CEO: Some prediction market traders bet Jensen Huang will make a comeback
st.teaser: Nvidia faces big risks because it has no succession plan and 60 executives report to Huang.
fullText: SINGAPORE – Jensen Huang has stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive , but some traders on the prediction market Kalshi are betting that the chipmaker will name him its next permanent CEO before 2029.
Nvidia has yet to name a permanent successor to one of the AI industry’s most influential leaders, with some in the industry calling him irreplaceable.

On Kalshi, which is regulated in the US but banned in Singapore, the implied odds of Nvidia naming Huang as its next permanent chief executive by the end of 2028 rose as high as 15% on the evening of Nov 13, before falling to around 7%.
Nvidia executive Ian Buck is currently in the lead, with a 33% chance on Kalshi of becoming Nvidia’s next CEO.

Buck is vice-president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing at Nvidia. He leads its multibillion-dollar data centre business, which supplies AI chips and software to major tech companies worldwide.
Kalshi put the odds of Colette Kress getting the permanent job at 13%. Kress is Nvidia’s chief financial officer and was made interim CEO following Huang’s resignation on Nov 12.
She is tied with Rene Haas, chief executive of British chip design company Arm Holdings.

Other executives Kalshi traders are betting on include Apple chief hardware officer Johny Srouji, Palo Alto Networks chairman and CEO Nikesh Arora, Nvidia executive vice-president Jay Puri, and AMD chairman and CEO Lisa Su. Puri oversees Nvidia’s global sales, business development and partnerships.

Tech executives, investors and fans have voiced support for Huang, who stepped down following reports of three affairs. He has admitted to being involved with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based, Alibaba-backed data centre firm Megaspeed . She is suspected by the US of spying for China.

“Jensen is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, wrote in an X post on Nov 8. He concluded that Nvidia’s Huang is “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership”.
About an hour later, Elon Musk quoted the post, noting: “I agree.”
Maguire added on Nov 12 that Huang’s ousting “will leave a huge void, with the loss of a technical, aggressive, founder-CEO.
“The American AI community needs to work double-time in an attempt to fill this void.”
Even US President Donald Trump called Huang before he stepped down, urging him to keep fighting for his job , according to The New York Times, quoting sources familiar with the call.

After Huang announced his resignation, Trump wrote in a Nov 12 Truth Social post : “Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – Tim Cook of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!”
On prediction market Polymarket, trading implied a 6% chance that Nvidia would name Apple executive chairman Tim Cook as its next permanent chief executive by the end of 2028.
There is also a 11% probability on Polymarket that Nvidia does not find a CEO by Dec 31, 2028.
Regardless of who takes over, Nvidia’s stakes are high because so much of the AI industry relies on chips, delivered by a company that Huang co-founded, transformed and led for the past 30 years.
A total of 60 executives across the firm report directly to him, and there is no succession plan.
Huang’s departure therefore leaves Nvidia investors weighing several risks, Saxo UK investor strategist Neil Wilson said in a Nov 13 note.
Nvidia is “about to find out whether Huang’s grip on the company and flat organisational structure was effectively storing up trouble”, said Wilson.
While a successor could keep Nvidia on the same course, Huang’s detailed knowledge of its products and his hands-on management style is unique and would be hard to replicate.

Wilson also pointed to scrutiny in Washington, citing reported US Justice Department inquiries involving Megaspeed and Alice Huang, and a request by three House committee chairs for a closed-door briefing on Nov 18 over national security concerns.
He expects Nvidia’s relationship with Washington to become more difficult, even with US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s support.

Investors, however, appear to think otherwise. Shares of Nvidia, which had fallen from around US$200 to a low of US$150 at the time of Huang’s ousting on Nov 12, have since rebounded and last traded at around US$162 each.
Brokers said trading in Nvidia surged after Huang’s resignation.

According to The Business Times, Nvidia orders at Syfe hit 13 times their six-week daily average in Singapore, while volume at FSM Global reached 11 times its October daily average. At IG, trading volume among Singapore clients rose nearly sixfold from the previous week.
Nvidia still has an edge after Huang’s departure. Its chips are powerful, many developers already use its software to build and run AI models, and it has longstanding ties with major customers.
Still, the lack of a credible succession plan could force Nvidia’s board, and investors, to reassess how much of the company’s future depends on Huang personally.
“He cannot be replaced, but a great CEO can also be found and take the company in a similar direction,” said Wilson.

cna.headline: Figure skating-Malinin leads Skate America short program in season debut
cna.teaser: Figure skating-Malinin leads Skate America short program in season debut
fullText: EVERETT, WASHINGTON, Nov 14 : American Ilia Malinin shrugged off a minor error to lead the men's short program at Skate America in Everett, Washington, on Friday in his first competition since winning a third world title in March.
The 21-year-old scored 96.74 points to open a 5.45-point advantage over Japan's Sota Yamamoto, while Mexico's Donovan Carrillo sat third with 86.49 points heading into Saturday's free skate.
Malinin landed a quadruple flip and a triple Axel but made a mistake on his quadruple Lutz, putting a hand down on the ice and managing only a double toe-loop combination.
The error proved costly only on paper as the American's superior technical score kept him comfortably clear of the field.
"I definitely felt a lot of support behind that short program. I feel like as the season goes on, this short program is going to be really easy to skate."
The three-time world champion began his campaign directly on the Grand Prix circuit after opting against competing at a lower-level event earlier in the season.

Malinin enters the new campaign looking to move on from a dramatic 2025-26 season in which his 14-event winning streak came to an end at the Winter Olympics, where he finished eighth overall in the singles competition.
The disappointment proved short-lived, however, as he rebounded weeks later in Prague to secure a third successive world title.
After Skate America, Malinin is scheduled to compete at the NHK Trophy, where he will bid to secure a place at December's Grand Prix Final, an event he has won in each of the last three seasons.

economistArticle.title: Where to find the anti-AI trade: The worse chipmakers do, the better Indian equities perform
paras: Global financial markets have been dominated by the relentless rise of artificial intelligence stocks, particularly semiconductor powerhouses. Yet for fund managers seeking a hedge against tech-driven volatility, an intriguing inverse relationship has emerged in South Asia. As enthusiasm for hardware giants occasionally stumbles, Indian equities are quietly carving out a niche as the ultimate anti-AI play.

The logic underpinning this dynamic hinges on capital allocation and commodity pricing. High-flying technology hardware manufacturers soak up immense liquidity in global portfolios, drawing funds away from emerging markets with alternative growth drivers. When profit-taking occurs in the semiconductor sector, institutional investors frequently redistribute their gains into stable domestic consumer markets like India.

Furthermore, the massive computing infrastructure required for artificial intelligence consumes vast amounts of energy and capital expenditure, which can inflate global energy costs and squeeze corporate margins elsewhere. India, primarily a service-driven economy with limited hardware manufacturing exposure, remains insulated from tech-supply bottlenecks while benefiting from lower input costs when hardware rallies cool off.

Local macroeconomic fundamentals also fortify this hedge. Driven by robust internal consumption, infrastructure expansion, and a rapidly growing middle class, Indian shares offer sustained momentum independent of Silicon Valley earnings cycles. While chipmakers fret over order volumes and geopolitical trade restrictions, Indian firms draw strength from domestic policy support.

Consequently, international investors looking to diversify away from concentrated tech positions are finding solace in Mumbai. Treating Indian equities as a counterweight to AI volatility may not only preserve capital during tech drawdowns, but also deliver consistent long-term growth rooted in real-economy fundamentals.
economistArticle.cn: 全球金融市场一直由人工智能概念股（尤其是半导体巨头）的持续上涨所主导。然而，对于希望规避科技股波动风险的基金经理而言，南亚市场出现了一种有趣的反向关联。每当市场对硬件巨头的热情偶尔遭遇挫折时，印度股市正悄然塑造出作为终极“反AI对冲”的独特地位。支撑这一动态的逻辑在于资本配置与商品定价。高歌猛进的科技硬件制造商吸收了全球投资组合中的巨额流动性，将资金从拥有其他增长引擎的新兴市场吸走。当半导体板块出现获利回吐时，机构投资者往往会将收益重新分配到像印度这样稳定的本土消费市场。此外，人工智能所需的庞大计算基础设施消耗了大量能源和资本支出，这可能推高全球能源成本并挤压其他行业的利润率。印度作为一个主要由服务业驱动、硬件制造参与度有限的经济体，在硬件热潮降温时，既能免受科技供应链瓶颈的影响，又能从较低的投入成本中受益。本土的宏观经济基本面也进一步巩固了这一对冲逻辑。在强劲的内部消费、基础设施扩张和快速增长的中产阶级推动下，印度股票提供了独立于硅谷盈利周期的持续增长动能。当芯片制造商为订单量和地缘政治贸易限制感到焦虑时，印度企业则从本土政策支持中吸取力量。因此，寻求摆脱高度集中科技头寸的国际投资者正在孟买找到安慰。将印度股票作为应对AI波动的平衡力量，不仅可以在科技股回撤期间保全资本，还能带来立足于实体经济基本面的稳定长期增长。
